title: The Ruler from Bethlehem
sum: Jerusalem is under siege and its judge is struck on the cheek. Then the voice turns: from Bethlehem, a village too small to count among Judah's clans, the LORD will bring out a ruler for Israel whose origins reach back to the distant past. He will shepherd by the LORD's strength, be great to the ends of the earth, and be peace when Assyria invades. English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:14, so this chapter starts one verse earlier in the Hebrew Bible.

The rest of the chapter has two pictures of the remnant of Jacob: dew that no human controls, and a lion among sheep. It ends with the LORD cutting away what Judah trusted: horses, chariots, fortresses, sorcery, carved images, standing stones and Asherah poles. The promise of a ruler and the removal of false security go together. Matthew 2:5-6 quotes verse 2 when the scribes tell Herod where the Messiah is to be born.
readings: Read as hope for a Davidic king

Verse 2 looks past a failed court to David's own village and promises a new king from David's line. The ruler shepherds, brings peace, and defeats Assyria through a team of capable leaders (5:5-6). The remnant chapters follow because his rule makes them safe.
Read as a message to Hezekiah's Judah

In 701 BC Sennacherib shut up Hezekiah in Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:13-19:36). A prophet could say that the king's rule is shaken, but the LORD's promise to David stands, and Assyria will not have the last word. The final section matches Hezekiah's reform (2 Kings 18:4).
Read as a unit within a longer book

Chapters 4-5 are a hopeful block set between the judgment of chapter 3 and the lawsuit of chapter 6. Critical readers ask which parts are Micah's and which were added; the chapter is still a single movement from siege to ruler to remnant to cleansing.

views.H: The setting is the Assyrian crisis, with 701 BC the likeliest moment for the siege of 5:1. Hezekiah was Judah's king (2 Kings 18); Bethlehem was David's home town. The 'ruler' is a future king of David's line, and in the history of Judah, readers have seen Hezekiah, a later Davidide or the Messiah. Assyria's fall (612 BC) did not end the empire problem, and the passage was read again under Babylon, Persia and Rome.
views.C: Critical commentators divide on how much of 4-5 is Micah's. Wellhausen is reported to have judged most of it later; Wolff, Mays and Hillers divide the chapters among Micah and later editors and differ on where the lines fall; Andersen-Freedman and Waltke defend most of it for Micah. Some who see later layers in chapters 4-5 still give verse 2 to Micah or his circle, because its contrast with Jerusalem's rulers fits chapter 3. The reference to Babylon in 4:10 is the book's most debated evidence for a later date. The Greek and Hebrew differ in 5:1, 5, 6 and 7.
views.J: The Targum Jonathan is reported to read 5:2 of the Messiah (from you the Messiah will come out before me, whose name was spoken from of old), and Rashi is reported to read the ruler as the Messiah son of David. The Talmud (Sukkah 52b) names the seven shepherds (Adam, Seth, Methuselah, Abraham, Jacob and Moses, with David in the middle) and eight princes of 5:5; the Talmud (Pesachim 54a) lists the name of the Messiah among seven things made before the world. Readers who follow 4:9-10 take the 'woman in labor' of 5:3 as Zion or Israel in the pains before redemption.
views.X: Matthew 2:4-6 has the scribes answer Herod with this verse, and John 7:42 shows people expected the Messiah from Bethlehem. Justin Martyr, Origen and Jerome cite it for Jesus' birth; Jerome and Cyril of Alexandria also hear his eternal generation in 'from days of old'. Luke 2:4 places Jesus in David's town. Some later readers, for example Jerome, connect the 'woman in labor' with Mary (compare Isaiah 7:14; Matthew quotes Isaiah there, not Micah 5:3). Verse 5, 'this one will be peace', is joined with Ephesians 2:14.
views.F: Dispensational readers take the first part of 5:2 as fulfilled at Jesus' birth and 5:3-15 as still to come: Israel is 'given up' until Christ's return, then regathered, defeating her enemies and cleansed of idols. Others read the whole passage as fulfilled in Jesus and the church ('the remnant of Jacob' as the believers among the nations). The verse gives no date.

deep.b:
Three scenes follow one another. 5:1-6 sets a besieged city and a shamed judge beside a ruler who comes from a village; the ruler shepherds, brings peace, and meets Assyria with human leaders. 5:7-9 turns to 'the remnant of Jacob', first as dew and then as a lion. 5:10-15 is one long sentence in the LORD's voice: 'I will cut off' (five times), 'I will tear down', 'I will pull up', 'I will take vengeance'. The Plain English Translation keeps 'cut off' every time so the repeated verb shows.

The chapter is also a bridge. Chapter 4 ended with Zion in labor (4:9-10). Chapter 5 begins with a siege and then gives the birth (5:3). Chapter 6 will turn the LORD's voice against his people in a courtroom.

Matthew 2:5-6 is a changed quotation, not a copy. It drops 'Ephrathah', changes 'too small' into 'in no way the least', reads 'leaders' for 'clans', adds 'for', and adds the line 'one who will shepherd my people Israel' from 2 Samuel 5:2. The note on 5:2 lists each difference. The point of Matthew's version is the reversal: the small town is great because of who comes from it. Micah's own point is similar, but it has no 'in no way'. Most scholars treat the differences as free quotation, a matter of how the early church quoted Scripture, not of a different Hebrew text; a few argue that Matthew used another textual or targumic form. The note on 5:2 lists eight differences, including the added 'for'.

echoes: Matthew 2:1-6; Matthew 2:4; John 7:42; Luke 2:4-11; 2 Samuel 5:2; 2 Samuel 7:8-16; Genesis 35:19; Ruth 4:11; 1 Samuel 17:12; Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 9:6-7; Isaiah 11:1; Ezekiel 34:23; Numbers 23:24; Genesis 49:9; Zechariah 9:10; Deuteronomy 17:16; Deuteronomy 18:10; 2 Kings 18:4; 2 Kings 18:13

settings.what: The siege and the ruler from Bethlehem
settings.by: The prophet Micah, speaking for the LORD (1:1)
settings.to: Judah and Jerusalem, in a siege or under the threat of one
settings.when: Debated. Most who accept it as Micah's place it in the Assyrian crisis, 701 BC. Critical commentators who date it later place it in or after the Babylonian siege of 586 BC.
settings.why: To tell a frightened city that its failed king is not the end. The LORD will bring out a ruler from David's own town, one who shepherds in the LORD's strength and who is 'peace' when Assyria comes. Knowing the audience changes the reading: a besieged city is promised a king who does not come from the siege.
views: A word to Hezekiah's Jerusalem during Sennacherib's campaign. The 'judge' is Hezekiah or his officials, and the new ruler is a coming Davidide.
A word to exiles or to Judah after 586, added to Micah's book. The 'judge' is Zedekiah and the ruler is the hoped-for Davidic king.

settings.what: The remnant as dew and as a lion
settings.to: The survivors of Jacob, among many peoples
settings.when: As verses 1-6, at the time of the siege or after it
settings.why: To tell a scattered, small people that they have a role among the nations. The remnant is a gift (dew) and a force (a lion). It lives not by human help but by the LORD.
settings.readers: Those who read the book later, in exile or after, would hear 'among many peoples' as their own life among foreign nations.

settings.what: The LORD clears out what Judah trusted
settings.to: Judah (the 'you') and, in verse 15, the nations
settings.when: 'On that day', a day the prophet does not date
settings.why: To remove Judah's false security: war-horses, chariots, fortified cities, magic and idols. The cleansing is meant to leave the people with the LORD alone. A listener who trusted the walls of Hezekiah's Jerusalem would hear this as a threat and a promise at once.

traditions.q: Is Micah 5:2 a direct prophecy of Jesus' birth, and how do the churches read Matthew's changed quotation?
views: The Lectionary for Mass is reported to read Micah 5:1-4a (the Catholic numbering of these verses) as the first reading on the Fourth Sunday of Advent in Year C, pointing the verse to Christ's birth. Jerome, in his commentary, reads it of Christ born in Bethlehem and hears his eternal origin in 'from days of old'. The Catechism's teaching that the literal sense is the base for the spiritual senses (115-119) is the frame for reading an Old Testament promise as fulfilled in Christ; it does not name Micah. No Catholic statement on Matthew's changed wording is cited here.

Micah 4:6-7 and 5:2-4 are reported among the Old Testament readings at Vespers of the Nativity (Festal Menaion), read of Christ's birth in Bethlehem. Cyril of Alexandria, a Father the Orthodox Church honors, hears the eternal generation of the Son in 'from days of old'. No Orthodox statement on Matthew's changed wording is cited here.

The Lutheran Service Book is reported to assign Micah 5:2-5a as the Old Testament reading for the Fourth Sunday in Advent in Series C of its three-year lectionary, which reads the verse of Christ's coming. No Lutheran statement on Matthew's changed wording is cited here.

Calvin, in his comment on Micah 5:2, reads the verse as a direct prophecy of Christ, with a human origin in David's line and a divine one in 'from days of old'. He is reported to treat Matthew's wording as giving the sense of the prophecy and not a different text; the exact passage was not re-read for this card.
No Baptist source on this verse has been checked for this card, so none is claimed.

Reported as the usual dispensational pattern (Pentecost, Things to Come, is the standard handbook; the section on Micah was not checked here): verse 2 is fulfilled at Jesus' birth, verse 3 ('he will hand them over until...') marks the span between his first coming and Israel's regathering, and verses 4-15 are still future, when the remnant is restored and cleansed.

title: The LORD Takes His People to Court
sum: A third speech begins with the same call as the first two: Hear. The LORD brings a case against his people before the mountains and hills, and asks, 'What have I done to you?' He answers his own question with the Exodus, the three leaders he sent, and the story of Balak and Balaam. The people reply with the question of all religion: what must I bring? A calf? A thousand rams? My firstborn?

The answer is short (6:8): do justice, love loyal love, and walk with your God in humility. The second half of the chapter then names the city's crimes: short measures, false weights, violence, lies, and the rules of Omri and Ahab. The punishment is the reverse of the covenant's blessings: you will sow and not reap.
readings: Read as a lawsuit (a form many scholars call the covenant lawsuit, though some doubt it was a fixed form): plaintiff, defendant, witnesses (the mountains), the history of benefits, the charge, the sentence. The LORD argues the case instead of simply condemning.
Read as a dialogue in the temple

Some readers hear a liturgy: a priest or prophet states the LORD's complaint (6:1-5), a worshipper asks what to bring (6:6-7), and a prophet or priest answers (6:8). The liturgy has the form of a torah entrance question like Psalm 15 and Psalm 24.
Verse 8 states that God wants justice, loyal love and a humble walk. The chapter does not say sacrifice is wrong, but it says it does not replace the three things God asks.

views.H: Micah's Judah in Hezekiah's time had cheating merchants and rich men who took the poor's land (2:1-2), a habit the book links with Omri and Ahab's dynasty (1 Kings 21). Child sacrifice was practiced by Ahaz (2 Kings 16:3). The reference to Balaam, Shittim and Gilgal recalls Israel's history before the land, which a 700s audience knew from their traditions.
views.C: Critical scholars debate whether 6:1-8 and 6:9-16 are one piece (a lawsuit and then its sentence) or two. Chapter 6:9-16 has some of the hardest Hebrew in the book (verses 9, 10, 11, 14). The reference to the 'statutes of Omri' has been dated to the 8th century (Micah) or later. Verse 8 is widely called the best summary of the prophets' ethics in one sentence; Mays and Wolff both read it as the answer to the questions of 6:6-7.
views.J: The Talmud (Makkot 23b-24a) says Micah reduced the 613 commandments to three; Sukkah 49b explains them as justice, acts of loving-kindness and modesty (quiet deeds such as escorting the dead). The mention of Miriam is used in the rabbinic story of the well that followed Israel for her sake (Taanit 9a).
views.X: Jesus' charge to the scribes and Pharisees about 'the heavier things in the law' (Matthew 23:23) matches the three of 6:8. Christians have disagreed on how verse 8 relates to grace: as the law's summary that shows our need of Christ (Luther's use of the law), as the shape of the life of the saved (Calvin's third use), or as part of the way of salvation (Catholic and Orthodox cooperation). The card on this chapter sets the churches side by side.
views.F: Few readers find future prediction in this chapter. The punishments of 6:13-16 are read as the covenant curses that came true in 722 and 586.

deep.h: From the courtroom to the temple
deep.b: The chapter has three steps. 6:1-5: the LORD asks what he has done, then lists his acts: the Exodus, the leaders, and the turning of Balaam's curse into blessing. 6:6-7: a voice asks what to bring and escalates to the unthinkable. 6:8: the answer is a short sentence that is also a list of verbs: do, love, walk. Verses 9-16 then give the particular charges against the city, from false measures to the rules of Omri. The movement is from God's past kindness, to human religion, to the daily life of a city.

Verse 7 should not be read as a gentle exaggeration only. Ahaz had burned his son (2 Kings 16:3), and Manasseh would (2 Kings 21:6). The law forbids it (Leviticus 18:21) and commands redemption of the firstborn (Exodus 13:13). Micah's questioner is at the end of his list of gifts and is asking whether the highest price must be paid. Micah's answer (6:8) does not mention the child at all. Jeremiah 7:31 has the LORD say outright that he never commanded it.

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2-20; Hosea 4:1; Hosea 6:6; Jeremiah 2:4-13; Exodus 20:2; Exodus 15:20; Numbers 22-24; Numbers 25:1; Joshua 4:19; Deuteronomy 10:12-13; Amos 5:21-24; Matthew 23:23; Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-16; Amos 8:5; 1 Kings 16:25-33; 1 Kings 21; 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6; Jeremiah 7:31; Leviticus 26:26; Deuteronomy 28:38-40

settings.what: The LORD's lawsuit and the answer to the worshipper
settings.by: The prophet Micah, summoning the LORD's case; then the LORD speaking in the first person (6:3-5); then a worshipper (6:6-7); then the prophet (6:8)
settings.to: Israel and Judah, the 'people' of 6:2, and the mountains and hills as the court
settings.when: Not dated. The book places all its speeches in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1).
settings.why: To remind a people of what the LORD has already done for them, so that they hear the charge as an offense against a faithful God, and to answer, in one sentence, the question of what real worship is. A listener who thinks religion is a matter of offerings hears that God asks for what a person does in the city.
views: A prophetic imitation of a court case between the LORD and his people, with the mountains as witnesses (Huffmon, Wright).
A temple or festival dialogue between priest, people and prophet (Gunkel's line).

settings.what: The charge against the city and its sentence
settings.to: The city (Jerusalem or Samaria's heirs) and its merchants and rich
settings.why: To name the daily crimes (false weights, violence, lies) that the earlier question about offerings left out, and to announce the covenant curses that follow. The people who gave offerings but cheated at the market are told that God sees the scales.
views: The city is Jerusalem, and the rules of Omri are a reference to Judah copying the northern dynasty (Athaliah, Ahaz).
The mention of Omri and Ahab, kings of Samaria, has led some to take the city as Samaria, with the oracle from before 722 BC; others prefer Jerusalem, since the book is addressed to Judah.

traditions.q: Micah 6:8 says what God asks: do justice, love loyal love, walk with your God in humility. None of the texts below comments on this verse; they show how each church's teaching on good works frames a verse like it. Is such a life the way of salvation, the duty of the saved, or a standard that shows our need of grace?
views: Justice, mercy and humility are works of charity done in grace. The Council of Trent teaches that the justified increase in righteousness by good works done through God's grace and keep the commandments (Session 6, chapters 10-11), and the Catechism (2006-2011) describes merit as itself a gift of grace.

As Ware describes the Orthodox view, salvation is union with God in which a person cooperates with grace (synergy). Acts of mercy and justice are part of the life of that union, not a payment for it. No Orthodox teacher is cited on this verse.

The verse states the law, which shows that no one does these things as God requires; people are justified by faith for Christ's sake, and good works follow as the fruit of faith (Augsburg Confession, articles 4, 6 and 20; Apology, article 4).

Good works are the fruits and evidence of a true faith, never its ground. The law remains a rule of life for believers (Westminster Confession, chapters 16 and 19; Heidelberg Catechism, questions 86-87).
The Second London Baptist Confession (1689), chapter 16, says that good works done in obedience to God's commandments are the fruits and evidences of a true faith.

title: Who Is a God Like You?
sum: The book ends in lament, trust and praise. The speaker finds no loyal person left in the land (7:1-6): officials, judges and the powerful twist justice, and even a household is not safe. Then comes a turn: 'I, though, will keep watch for the LORD.' The speaker confesses sin and waits for the LORD to take up his case; the enemy who said 'Where is your God?' will be trampled.

A day of rebuilding walls is promised, and people come from every side (7:11-13). A prayer asks the LORD to shepherd his flock as in the days of the Exodus, and he answers with wonders. The book closes with a hymn built on the prophet's own name, Micah, 'Who is like the LORD?': a God who forgives guilt, delights in loyal love, throws every sin into the depths of the sea, and keeps the oath he swore to Abraham and Jacob.
readings: The chapter is a prophetic liturgy with many voices: lament, trust, confession, divine promise, prayer, divine answer, praise. The movement from despair to praise is the movement of the whole book.

7:1-6 (a lament), 7:7-10 (a song of trust), 7:11-13 (a promise), 7:14-17 (a prayer and answer) and 7:18-20 (a hymn) may be separate texts joined by editors, with the last in the exilic or later period.
Read as the end of the Twelve's sixth book
In the Hebrew order of the Twelve the book ends on the creed of Exodus 34:6-7, turned toward forgiveness. The next book, Nahum, takes up the same creed in its judging half.

views.H: 7:1-6 fits the world of Micah's earlier chapters: land-grabbing, corrupt judges, no trust. 7:11-13 may speak of the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, which fits Hezekiah's repair (2 Chronicles 32:5) or Nehemiah's rebuilding (Nehemiah 2-6). The enemy 'she who said, Where is your God?' (7:10) has been identified with Assyria, Babylon or Edom.
views.C: Many critical scholars date 7:8-20, or all of 7:7-20, to the exile or later. Reasons: the speaker is a community in darkness (7:8-9), the walls are down (7:11), and the people are scattered and wait for return (7:12, 14-15). The conservative reply is that Micah could speak in the voice of the people under threat, as Isaiah does. Gunkel read the end of the book as a liturgy. The Greek and Hebrew differ in 7:3, 11, 12, 19.
views.J: 7:18-20 is the haftarah for Shabbat Shuvah, the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, in many rites (with Hosea 14), and the custom of tashlich (casting sins into water) draws on 7:19. Mishnah Sotah 9:15 quotes 7:6 among the signs before the Messiah. The Talmud (Makkot 23b-24a) counts 6:8 as the verse in which Micah reduced the commandments to three.
views.X: Jesus quotes 7:6 in Matthew 10:35-36 and Luke 12:53. Christian readers hear the shepherd of 7:14 fulfilled in Jesus (John 10:11). The Roman lectionary reads 7:14-15, 18-20 on the Saturday of the second week of Lent with the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15). The card on this chapter sets the churches side by side.
views.F: 7:11-17 is read as a picture of the last days: walls rebuilt, nations coming to the LORD, a new Exodus with wonders, enemies crawling like snakes. Dispensational readers see the regathering of Israel; amillennial readers the church; others a final restoration of all peoples (compare 4:1-3). 7:18-20 states the ground of every future hope: the oath to Abraham.

deep.h: The name Micah and the question
deep.b: The prophet's name means "Who is like Yah?" (it appears as Mikhayah in the written text of Jeremiah 26:18, and in the longer form Mikhayahu for other men of the name). Verse 18 asks mi El kamokha, 'Who is a God like you?' The book ends on the same question that its writer's name asks, and the question is answered by what follows: a God who forgives, does not stay angry, delights in loyal love, and keeps his oath. The same words come in the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:11), where the question is about power over Egypt. Micah answers it about forgiveness.

deep.h: How the book turns three times
deep.b: Micah has three 'Hear' speeches (1:2; 3:1; 6:1), and each moves from accusation to hope. Chapters 1-2 end with the remnant gathered (2:12-13). Chapters 3-5 end with a ruler and a purified land (4-5). Chapters 6-7 end with the pardoning God (7:18-20). The strongest judgment is followed by the largest promise. Readers who take the book as a unit see this as its design; readers who see editing see it as the shape the editors gave it.

echoes: Exodus 34:6-7; Exodus 15:5; Exodus 15:11; Numbers 14:18-19; Psalm 103:8-12; Psalm 12:1; Psalm 28:9; Jeremiah 26:18; Jeremiah 5:1; Jeremiah 9:4; Hosea 14:2; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Nahum 1:2-3; Genesis 12:1-3; Genesis 22:16-18; Genesis 28:13-15; Luke 1:72-73; Matthew 10:35-36; Luke 12:53; Luke 15:20; Mishnah Sotah 9:15

settings.what: A lament in a land with no loyal person
settings.by: A speaker, probably the prophet, for the faithful remnant or for Zion
settings.to: The community, and the LORD who hears
settings.when: The days of Micah's earlier chapters, or later
settings.why: To say aloud that the land has no loyal person left, so that the hearers may feel what the prophet feels, and to prepare for the turn of 7:7. The listener who hears 'do not trust a neighbor' is a listener who knows it is true.

settings.what: Trust, confession and the answer to the enemy
settings.by: The same speaker, or Zion personified
settings.to: The LORD, and the enemy who gloats
settings.why: To show how to wait: admit guilt, bear the anger, and trust the LORD to take up the case. The enemy is told not to gloat.
views: The prophet speaks for himself and the faithful.
Zion personified, as in Lamentations, speaks to her enemy.
The community in exile, where 'Where is your God?' was a daily taunt.

settings.by: A prophetic voice, speaking for the LORD (in the second person to the city)
settings.to: Zion, pictured as a woman, whose walls are to be rebuilt
settings.why: To tell a city in ruins or in danger that its walls will be rebuilt and that people will come from every side. The sudden 'But' of 7:13 holds out a warning for those who will not come.

settings.what: A prayer for the shepherd, and the LORD's answer
settings.by: The prophet or the people (7:14), then the LORD (7:15), then the prophet (7:16-17)
settings.to: The LORD, who is asked to shepherd; and the nations
settings.why: To ask the LORD to do again what he did in the Exodus, and to hear his answer. For a people who felt they lived 'alone in a forest', it is the request of a flock that cannot defend itself.

settings.by: The people, led by the prophet (or the prophet alone, or an editor, if the hymn is a later addition)
settings.to: The LORD, in the second person
settings.when: Not dated; possibly sung in worship
settings.why: To end the book with a confession of what kind of God the LORD is: one who forgives, delights in loyal love and keeps his oath. For hearers who had just heard the threats of chapters 1-3, it answers whether judgment is the last word.
settings.readers: The pun on the prophet's name (Mikhayahu) tells later readers that the book of Micah is also a book about the question 'Who is like the LORD?'.

traditions.q: How does God forgive sin, and what does the church do about confession and absolution?
views: God forgives through the sacrament of Penance: the penitent confesses to a priest, who gives absolution in Christ's name (Catechism 1440-1449).
Confession is made before a priest, who stands as a witness while Christ forgives; the sacrament belongs to the Church's medicine for the soul.

Private confession and absolution are kept and valued, though the listing of every sin is not required; the absolution is God's own word of forgiveness spoken through the pastor (Augsburg Confession, articles 11 and 25; Small Catechism, 'Confession').

God alone forgives sin. Believers confess to God directly, and public confession belongs to church discipline; ministers declare God's pardon to the penitent from the Word (Westminster Confession, chapter 15; Heidelberg Catechism, question 84).
A believer confesses sin to God and is forgiven through Christ with no priest between; the church preaches the gospel's pardon (Second London Baptist Confession, chapter 15).
